algorithms.name: annual profection
algorithms.steps: Determine the native's age at the start of the year in question (age = whole years since birth). Compute profected house = (age mod 12) + 1, counting WHOLE-SIGN houses forward from the natal Ascendant's sign (house 1 = the ASC's own sign, regardless of the quadrant house system used for the main chart). The 'Lord of the Year' / time-lord is the TRADITIONAL ruler of that house's sign (Aries & Scorpio = Mars, Taurus & Libra = Venus, Gemini & Virgo = Mercury, Cancer = Moon, Leo = Sun, Sagittarius & Pisces = Jupiter, Capricorn & Aquarius = Saturn). Monthly profections advance one house per month starting from the year's house at the birth-month anniversary, cycling through the remaining 11 houses one per month, each with its own monthly sub-lord.
algorithms.inputs: Natal Ascendant sign (whole-sign reckoning, not the natal quadrant chart); current age or the specific year being profected; traditional (not modern) planetary rulerships.
algorithms.output_format: One Telegram line, e.g. 'Profection year: 10th house (Aries) -- Mars is your time-lord through Nov 2026.'

algorithms.name: firdaria
algorithms.steps: Determine day vs night birth from whether the natal Sun is above (day) or below (night) the ASC-DSC horizon line. For a NIGHT chart, the major periods run in this fixed order and length: Moon 9y, Saturn 11y, Jupiter 12y, Mars 7y, Sun 10y, Venus 8y, Mercury 13y, then North Node 3y, South Node 2y (75y total, then the whole cycle repeats). Sum the lengths cumulatively to find which major period the current age falls into. Within that major period, divide it into 7 equal sub-periods (major length / 7 years each); the major lord itself rules the first sub-period, then the sequence continues through the remaining six planets in Chaldean order (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon) picking up wherever the major lord sits in that order.
algorithms.inputs: Natal Sun's position relative to the ASC/DSC axis (to confirm night birth); exact birth date for the cumulative age-in-years math.
algorithms.output_format: One Telegram line, e.g. 'Firdaria: Mars major period (age 32-39) / Sun sub-period (through Nov 2026).'

algorithms.name: planetary hours
algorithms.steps: Get sunrise and sunset for the exact location and date. Diurnal hour length = (sunset minus sunrise) / 12. Nocturnal hour length = (next sunrise minus sunset) / 12. Hour 1 of the day (starting at sunrise) is ruled by that weekday's ruling planet (Sun=Sunday, Moon=Monday, Mars=Tuesday, Mercury=Wednesday, Jupiter=Thursday, Venus=Friday, Saturn=Saturday). Every subsequent hour, day and night together (24 total per 24-hour cycle), advances one step through the Chaldean order -- Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon -- wrapping continuously across the sunset boundary into the (differently-sized) night hours.
algorithms.inputs: Sunrise/sunset times for the exact location and date (ephemeris or sunrise-sunset API); the calendar weekday.
algorithms.output_format: One Telegram line, e.g. 'Right now: Venus hour (until 3:42pm) -- good for money/relationship conversations.'

algorithms.name: progressions and transits to progressed points
algorithms.steps: Secondary progressions use the day-for-a-year key: the chart cast for N days after birth describes age N; progressed planets move at their natural daily ephemeris speed compounded over age-in-days. Progressed angles (ASC/MC) need special handling since houses depend on geographic latitude and right ascension, not simple longitude. Two accepted methods, which diverge by roughly 2-6 degrees over a lifetime: (a) NAIBOD -- advance the natal ARMC by the Sun's MEAN daily motion (about 0.9856 deg/day) times age-in-years, then recompute ASC/MC from that new ARMC; (b) SOLAR ARC -- advance the MC by the Sun's ACTUAL longitude motion since birth (the 'solar arc'), then derive the new ASC from that MC's implied right ascension. Pick one method and stay consistent. TRANSIT-TO-MIDPOINT RULE: a transiting planet activates a natal midpoint (the exact mid-degree between two natal points, (pointA + pointB) / 2) the same way it activates an actual planet -- check the transiting longitude against the midpoint within a tight ~1 degree orb; a hit blends both points' themes at once.
algorithms.inputs: Natal ARMC and Sun longitude; current transiting planet positions; the two natal points defining any midpoint being checked.
algorithms.output_format: One Telegram line, e.g. 'Transiting Saturn is conjunct your progressed Moon -- expect a few weeks of emotional reckoning around [themed house].'

algorithms.name: lunar mansions (nakshatras)
algorithms.steps: Convert the Moon's TROPICAL longitude to SIDEREAL by subtracting the Lahiri ayanamsa value for the date in question (roughly 24 degrees in the current era, about 23.7 deg for 1992) -- do this for both the natal Moon and any daily transiting Moon position. Divide the 360-degree zodiac into 27 equal nakshatras of 13 deg 20' each, each further split into 4 padas of 3 deg 20'. Look up which of the 27 segments the sidereal longitude falls into to get the ruling planet (the fixed, repeating Vimshottari sequence: Ketu, Venus, Sun, Moon, Mars, Rahu, Jupiter, Saturn, Mercury -- repeated 3 times across the 27), presiding deity, and traditional nature/gana.
algorithms.inputs: Tropical Moon longitude (natal or transiting) and the correct Lahiri ayanamsa value for the date in question.
algorithms.output_format: One Telegram line, e.g. 'Moon is in Shatabhisha today -- good for solitary research/healing work, not for public launches.'

algorithms.name: planetary returns
algorithms.steps: For any body, a 'return' is the moment its transiting longitude exactly matches its natal longitude again. Approximate cycle lengths: Moon ~27.3 days, Mercury/Venus ~1 year (count varies with retrograde loops), Mars ~2 years, Jupiter ~12 years, Saturn ~29.5 years, Chiron ~50 years (its eccentric orbit makes exact timing variable), Uranus ~84 years; the lunar NODES complete a full 360-degree retrograde cycle back to the natal position roughly every 18.6 years (called a 'nodal return' by the same convention even though the nodes move backward). Because none of these orbits are perfectly uniform, get the exact date from ephemeris lookup (e.g. pyswisseph) rather than simple division -- a body near a retrograde station can produce more than one exact hit per nominal cycle.
algorithms.inputs: Natal longitude of the body in question; an ephemeris capable of solving for the exact transiting-to-natal conjunction date(s).
algorithms.output_format: One Telegram line, e.g. 'Mars return: [date] -- new 2-year action cycle begins.'
